topic: Improving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for question answering

selected_papers.title: ChunkRank: Relevance-Weighted Passage Selection for RAG
selected_papers.abstract: We propose ChunkRank, a lightweight reranking step that scores retrieved passages by relevance to the query before they are shown to a generation model. On two short-context QA benchmarks, ChunkRank improves answer accuracy over a standard top-k retrieval baseline, with a small added latency cost from the reranking step. All experiments use single-hop, English-language questions.

selected_papers.title: LongMem: Compressive Memory for Multi-Hop Retrieval
selected_papers.abstract: LongMem introduces a compressive memory module that lets a retrieval system summarize and reuse information across multiple retrieval hops instead of re-retrieving from scratch each time. On a multi-hop QA benchmark, LongMem improves accuracy over single-hop retrieval baselines, but adds noticeably higher inference latency due to the memory compression step. Evaluation is limited to English-language corpora.

selected_papers.title: CiteGuard: Faithfulness Verification for Generated Answers
selected_papers.abstract: CiteGuard is a post-hoc verifier that checks whether each sentence of a generated answer is actually supported by the retrieved passages it cites, flagging unsupported sentences before the answer is shown to a user. Applying CiteGuard reduces the rate of unsupported claims in generated answers, at the cost of an extra inference pass per answer. The verifier itself is not evaluated on multi-hop or non-English questions.

approved_web_articles.title: Why Chunk Ranking Matters for RAG Pipelines in Production
approved_web_articles.snippet: Teams running retrieval-augmented generation in production report that a simple relevance-ranking pass over retrieved chunks, before generation, meaningfully reduces off-topic citations -- without needing a larger retrieval model.

executive_summary.content: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, is a technique where a system first searches for relevant text passages and then uses a language model to write an answer grounded in those passages. This review covers three recent approaches to making RAG more accurate: reranking retrieved passages before generation, using compressive memory for multi-step questions, and verifying that generated answers are actually supported by their sources. Together, these approaches improve accuracy, but each adds some extra computation cost.

introduction_scope.content: Before comparing these approaches, two terms are worth defining. Retrieval is the step where a system searches a document collection for passages likely to contain the answer. Faithfulness (sometimes called groundedness) means that everything a generated answer states is actually backed up by the retrieved text, rather than invented by the model. This review covers exactly three papers selected for this topic: a passage-reranking method, a multi-hop memory method, and an answer-verification method. It does not attempt to cover retrieval-augmented generation more broadly.

thematic_findings.content: Two of the selected papers focus on giving the generation model better information to work with in the first place. ChunkRank re-scores retrieved passages for relevance right before generation, which improved answer accuracy on short, single-hop questions [1]. LongMem instead targets questions that need multiple retrieval steps, using a compressive memory so the system does not have to re-search from scratch at each step, which improved accuracy on multi-hop questions [2]. Read together, these two papers suggest that using retrieved information better -- whether by reordering individual passages or by remembering across steps -- reliably helps accuracy, even though they solve different parts of the retrieval problem.

sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.content: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, is a technique where a system first searches for relevant text passages and then uses a language model to write an answer grounded in those passages. This review covers three recent approaches to making RAG more accurate: reranking retrieved passages before generation, using compressive memory for multi-step questions, and verifying that generated answers are actually supported by their sources. Together, these approaches improve accuracy, but each adds some extra computation cost.

sections.title: Introduction & Scope

This review covers exactly three papers selected for this topic: a passage-reranking method, a multi-hop memory method, and an answer-verification method. It does not attempt to cover retrieval-augmented generation more broadly.

sections.title: Thematic Findings
sections.content: Two of the selected papers focus on giving the generation model better information to work with in the first place. ChunkRank re-scores retrieved passages for relevance right before generation, which improved answer accuracy on short, single-hop questions [1]. LongMem instead targets questions that need multiple retrieval steps, using a compressive memory so the system does not have to re-search from scratch at each step, which improved accuracy on multi-hop questions [2]. Read together, these two papers suggest that using retrieved information better -- whether by reordering individual passages or by remembering across steps -- reliably helps accuracy, even though they solve different parts of the retrieval problem.

sections.title: Methodology Landscape
sections.content: The three papers take different technical approaches to improving RAG. ChunkRank re-scores already-retrieved passages with a lightweight relevance-scoring step, applied as an add-on before generation [1]. Unlike ChunkRank's reranking step, LongMem changes what the retrieval system remembers between steps rather than re-scoring what it retrieves [1][2]. CiteGuard does not touch retrieval at all -- it checks the generated answer afterward, sentence by sentence, against the retrieved passages [3]. sections.title: Contradictions & Open Debates
sections.content: ChunkRank and LongMem each report an accuracy improvement [1], and CiteGuard reports a reduction in unsupported claims -- but all three add computation cost: LongMem's memory compression step adds noticeably higher latency [2], while CiteGuard's answer-checking step adds an entire extra pass over the generated answer [3]. None of the three papers directly compares its own benefit against its own added cost in a way that lets a reader judge whether the trade-off is worthwhile -- each paper reports its own benefit as justifying the added cost, but none puts a number on that trade-off directly.

sections.title: Gap Analysis
sections.content: All three papers evaluate only on English-language text, and none evaluates a multilingual or cross-lingual setting [1][2][3]. None of the three papers evaluates its method on more than one type of question difficulty at once -- ChunkRank is evaluated only on single-hop questions, LongMem only on multi-hop, and CiteGuard's verification step is not tested against multi-hop answers at all. There is also no joint accuracy-versus-cost measurement across all three techniques used together.

sections.title: Future Research Directions
sections.content: A natural next step is testing CiteGuard's answer-verification approach specifically on multi-hop answers, such as those produced by a LongMem-style system [2][3], since verification has so far only been tested on simpler answers. A second direction is extending any of these three methods to non-English text, since all three are currently English-only. Beyond the papers themselves, practitioner reports suggest that even a simple relevance-ranking step over retrieved passages helps in real deployments, which is consistent with what ChunkRank found in a research setting [1][4].

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content: Better passage selection, better multi-step retrieval, and after-the-fact verification each independently improve RAG systems, each at some added computational cost. A newcomer to this area should read the three approaches as complementary rather than competing: they act at different points in the pipeline.

citation_correctness.label: pass
citation_correctness.rationale: Every [N] marker sits next to the specific claim its source actually supports: [1] ChunkRank is cited only for passage reranking/single-hop accuracy, exactly what its abstract states; [2] LongMem only for multi-hop memory/latency; [3] CiteGuard only for post-hoc verification. No marker is attached to a claim its reference doesn't cover.

groundedness.label: pass
groundedness.rationale: Every factual claim (accuracy improved, added latency/cost, English-only evaluation scope) is directly traceable to a sentence in the corresponding abstract. No invented numbers, datasets, or results appear anywhere in the report.

synthesis_quality.label: pass
synthesis_quality.rationale: Thematic Findings groups ChunkRank and LongMem by shared theme (better use of retrieved passages) and states what they collectively show, rather than summarizing each paper in an isolated paragraph.

analytical_quality.label: pass
analytical_quality.rationale: Gap Analysis (no multilingual evaluation, no joint cost/accuracy measurement) is diagnostic; Future Research Directions turns those same gaps into concrete, distinct proposals (test CiteGuard on multi-hop, extend to non-English) rather than restating them verbatim.

template_fit.label: pass
template_fit.rationale: Foundational-appropriate: defines 'retrieval' and 'faithfulness' explicitly before using them, matching a newcomer's needs, without extraneous jargon.

coherence.label: pass
coherence.rationale: No repeated sentences across sections; each section stays within its own stated scope (Gap Analysis stays diagnostic, Future Research Directions stays prescriptive).

source_balance.label: pass
source_balance.rationale: All three papers are cited multiple times across sections in roles matched to what they actually contribute; the one web source is used once, for supporting practitioner context, not as a substitute for a paper citation.

notes: Baseline 'good' fixture, foundational template. Shares the exact same 3 papers + 1 web article as good_analytical.json and good_expert.json so a reviewer can compare template depth directly against identical evidence -- only the prompt-driven prose style should differ, not the underlying claims or citations. All source evidence is synthetic and hand-written; no real publications are referenced. R6C.2b adjudication: after live report-quality runs (report_quality_history.csv run_ids 2 and 3, commits cf60191 and bf8541d) repeatedly found citation/grounding defects in this fixture's report prose despite its 'pass' expected labels, the prose was corrected -- removed an unsupported three-way latency superlative, corrected CiteGuard's reported metric (unsupported-claim reduction, not accuracy), added existing citations to two cross-source claims, replaced 'a separate relevance model' with language matching ChunkRank's actual abstract, and reworded the Thematic Findings opening/closing framing so it no longer describes LongMem's cross-hop memory mechanism as simply 'better passages'. R6C.2c: the post-adjudication live smoke (run_id 4, commit d0c4982) surfaced one remaining omission in Contradictions & Open Debates -- the sentence credited ChunkRank with an accuracy improvement and computation cost without citing [1] -- corrected by adding [1] alongside the existing [2][3]. Run_id 5 (commit ff67113) then exposed a further wording error in the same sentence: LongMem's latency clause incorrectly attached 'than a single-hop baseline' -- LongMem's abstract ties that baseline comparison only to its accuracy clause, not its latency clause -- corrected to 'adds noticeably higher latency [2]' with no baseline comparison. expected.dimension_labels was NOT changed.
